analytic.title: Efficient Scheduling of Independent Tasks Using Modified Heuristics

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: In heterogeneous computing systems MinMin and MaxMin are widely used in assigning independent tasks to processors. For N tasks to be assigned to N processors these approaches are known to run in O (KN 2 ) time. An algorithmic improvement that asymptotically decreases the running time complexity of MinMin to O(KN logN) without affecting its solution quality is proposed in [1]. The newly proposed MinMin algorithm is combined with MaxMin, resulting in two hybrid algorithms [1]. The first hybrid algorithm address the drawback of MaxMin in solving problem instances with highly skewed cost distributions while also improving the running time performance of MaxMin. The second hybrid algorithm improves the running time performance without degrading its solution quality. The proposed algorithms are easy to implement. For the large datasets used in the various experiments, MinMin and MaxMin, as well as recent state-of-the-art heuristics, require days, weeks, or even months to produce a solution, whereas the proposed algorithms in this paper produce solutions within only two or three minutes. The new modified algorithms namely MinMax and MinMax+ are proposed and implemented. These algorithms are compared with the existing algorithms MinMin and MaxMin on single objective cases.

div.head: INTRODUCTION
div.p: The independent task assignment problem is related to heterogeneous computing systems [1,2]. A set of N independent tasks are to be assigned to K heterogeneous processors, an expected time to compute is represented by matrix E = {x i,k } NxK . Here x i,k represents the execution cost of task i on processor k. The main objective is to minimize the turnaround time and utilize the available processing power by minimizing the load of overloaded processors. The MinMin heuristic is used many times for solving the independent task assignment problem, which commonly emerges in the context of heterogeneous systems [1]- [10]. MinMin has some desirable properties and it is termed as a constructive heuristic. As it does not require any tuning parameters, it is easy to implement. It produces high quality solutions. The running time of the MinMin algorithm is reported to be O(KN 2 ) [1], [4], [5], [8]- [13].

In problems where the number of tasks to be assigned is very large this heuristic can't be used due to the quadratic running time complexity. The parallel version of MinMin algorithm enables the application of the algorithm to large datasets [14]. The parallel version of MinMin runs in O(N 2 K/P+N 2 +N log P) time, where P denotes the number of homogenous processors used in parallelization of the MinMin algorithm. The computational complexity of MinMin is overlooked in the earlier research on parallel and distributed computing [17]. For a large dataset that contains about 2.5 million tasks, MinMin finds a 16-way assignment in about 22 days, whereas proposed algorithms finds the same assignment in less time.

The other well-known constructive heuristics used for solving the independent task assignment problem is MaxMin [1], [2], [8], [15][16][17]. This heuristic differs from MinMin in the task selection policy adopted during the task to-processor assignment process. In this paper, improvements over MinMin and MaxMin heuristics are proposed.

div.head: II. RELATED WORK
div.p: Real time systems can be categorized as hard real time and soft real time systems [1]. Hard real time systems are strict about adherence to each task deadline. An event, when it occurs, should be serviced within the predictable time at all times in a given hard real time system. For the hard real time task the preemption period in worst case should be less than a few μ s. A hard real time system has predictable performance with no deadline miss, even in case of sudden bursts of occurrence of events requiring attention. Automobile engine control system, video transmission and anti lock brake system (ABS) [1,18] are some of the examples of hard real time systems. Some issues should be considered while designing hard real time systems: disabling of all other interrupts of lower priority when running the hard real time tasks, preemption of higher priority task by lower priority tasks, some critical code in assembly to meet the real time constraint fast, task running in kernel space (running any task in kernel space will reduce the time required to check whether access is outside the memory space allocated to the kernel functions), provision of asynchronous input and outputs, provision of locks or spin locks, predictions of interrupt latencies and context switching latencies of the tasks, predictability is achieved by writing all functions which execute always take the same predefined time intervals in case of varying rates of occurrences of the events. The given events should be responded in all the time slots in the system. A hard real time system provides the guaranteed task deadlines even in case of aperiodic tasks which doesn't have a definite period of event occurrence.

In contrast, in soft real time system deadlines are mostly met. Only the precedence and sequence for the task operations are defined. Interrupt latencies and context switching latencies are small but there can be few deviations between expected latencies of the tasks and observed time constraints and a few deadline misses are accepted. The preemption period for the soft real time task in worst case may be about a few m s. Digital cameras, mobile phones and orchestra playing robots are examples of soft real time systems. This can be identified that the design complexity of hard real time scheduling algorithms are higher as compared to soft real time scheduling algorithm.

A new method of bounding pre-emption costs, called the ECB-Union approach is introduced in [3,19]. This approach dominates the union cost bound (UCB) approach. The ECB-Union and UCB-Union approaches cannot be compared, therefore they are combined into a composite response time test that dominates the use of either approach. The ECB-Union and UCB-Union approaches are extended to systems that permit tasks to access shared resources in mutual exclusion as per the stack resource policy. Previous approaches to computing preemption delays did not account for the preemption of blocking tasks during a resource access, although including blocking factors in their schedulability analyses. This elimination leads to optimistic response times. This issue is addressed in [3]. The performance of the various approaches is examined to computing pre-emption costs using a case study and an empirical evaluation of task set schedulability. A combined response time analysis test using both the new ECB-Union approach and the UCB-Union approach provides an effective method of determining task schedulability. This approach offers a significant improvement in performance over previous approaches for a wide range of different task and cache configurations, on the basis of cache utilization level, amount of reuse, cache size, and block reload times.

The penalty of cache interference is bounded for real-time tasks by providing accurate predictions of data cache behavior across preemptions, including instruction cache and pipeline effects in [4,20]. It has been shown that the critical instant does not occur upon simultaneous release of all tasks while considering cache preemption. Analysis methods are developed to calculate upper bounds on the number of possible preemption points for each job of a task. To make these bounds tight, the entire range between the best-case and worst-case execution times (BCET and WCET) of higher priority jobs is considered. A feedback mechanism is used to interact with static timing analyzer the effects of cache interference are integrated into the WCET calculations. In [4] significant improvements in tightening bounds of up to an order of magnitude over two prior methods and up to half a magnitude over a third prior method are obtained by experiments for the number of preemptions, the WCET and the response time of a task. The work presented in [4] contributes by calculating the worst-case preemption delay under consideration of data caches. One can quantify the effect of phasing on bounding feasible preemption points.

A framework that provides safe and tight bounds of the data-cache related preemption delay (D-CRPD), the WCET and the worst-case response times, not just for homogeneous tasks under fully preemptive or fully non-preemptive systems, but for tasks with a non-preemptive region is proposed in [5]. Task sets become schedulable by retaining the option of preemption where legal. Correctness is ensured in terms of arbitration of access to shared resources by requiring a region within a task to be non-preemptive. Experimental results confirmed an increase in schedulability of a task set with non preemptive regions over an equivalent task set where only those tasks with non-preemptive regions are scheduled nonpreemptively. D-CRPD bounds and response-time bounds comparable to task sets with fully non-preemptive tasks can be retained in the presence of short non-preemptive regions. [5] is the first framework that performs D-CRPD calculations in a system for tasks with a non-preemptive region. A framework to calculate safe and tight timing bounds of data-cache related preemption delay and worst-case response times is presented in [5,21]. In contrast to past work, this approach handles tasks with a non-preemptive region of execution. Through experiments, response-time bounds obtained for task sets where some tasks have non-preemptive regions. These results are compared to an equivalent task set where only those tasks with non-preemptive regions are scheduled non-preemptively altogether. For some task sets, schedulability is improved without significantly affecting the response times of tasks using partially non-preemptive tasks as opposed to fully nonpreemptive tasks.

The notion of preemption threshold to develop a new scheduling model is used in [10], which unifies the concepts of preemptive and non-preemptive scheduling, and subsumes both as special cases. The notion of preemption threshold was introduced by Express Logic, Inc. in their ThreadX real-time operating system. It allows a task to disable preemption from tasks up to a specified threshold priority. Tasks having priorities higher than the threshold are still allowed to preempt. In [10], each task has a regular priority and a preemption threshold. The scheduling model can be analyzed for response times. Algorithms for optimal assignment of priorities and preemption threshold are developed. The evidence that this scheduling model provides substantial quantitative benefits over both preemptive and nonpreemptive scheduling models is provided in [10]. The proposed model [10] can result in substantial improvement of schedulability by taking advantage of aspects of both preemptive and non-preemptive scheduling. It also provides lower run-time costs by eliminating unnecessary preemptions.

In [12] simple scheduling models have been extended to include realistic kernel features and necessary application requirements. A flexible computational model supported by a rich set of analysis techniques is presented. The real time systems designer now has the techniques available to engineer systems [12].

Fixed-priority scheduling with deferred preemption (FPDS) has been proposed as an alternative to fixed-priority pre-emptive scheduling (FPPS) that obviates the need for nontrivial resource access protocols and reduces the cost of arbitrary preemptions. It has been shown in [13] that existing worst-case response time analysis of hard real-time tasks under FPDS, arbitrary phasing and relative deadlines at most equal to periods is pessimistic and/or optimistic. The same problem also arises for fixed priority non-pre-emptive scheduling (FPNS), being a special case of FPDS. A revised analysis, resolving the problems with the existing approaches is presented in [13]. The analysis is based on known concepts of critical instant and busy period for FPPS. To accommodate for scheduling model for FPDS, it is need to slightly modify existing definitions of these concepts. The analysis assumed a continuous scheduling model, which is based on a partitioning of the timeline in a set of non-empty, right semi-open intervals. It is shown that the critical instant, longest busy period and worst-case response time for a task are suprema rather than maxima for all tasks, except for the lowest priority task, i.e. that instant, period, and response time cannot be assumed. Moreover, it is shown that the analysis is not uniform for all tasks, i.e. the analysis for the lowest priority task differs from the analysis of the other tasks. These anomalies for the lowest priority task are an immediate consequence of the fact that only the lowest priority task cannot be blocked. The worst-case response time analysis for FPDS is expressed in terms of known worst-case analysis results for FPPS. Pessimistic variants of the analysis, which are uniform for all tasks is included in [13]. In this paper section II describes the limited preemptive scheduling for combining preemptive and non preemptive scheduling, in terms of preemption threshold scheduling (PTS), deferred preemption scheduling (DPS) and fixed preemption points (FPP). Section III describes the implementation issues related to PTS, DPS and FPP. Section IV describes the predictability. Section IV also provides the comparative analysis of limited preemptive scheduling approaches on the basis of average number of preemptions versus utilization, feasible task sets versus utilization, average number of preemptions versus number of tasks, feasible task sets versus number of tasks and feasible ratio versus utilization under different values.

div.head: III. EXISTING INDEPENDENT TASK ASSIGNMENT ALGORITHMS
div.p: The MinMin has N iterations. Unassigned task is selected and assigned to a processor. The remaining iterations do not consider this assigned task. The assignment of task to processor each iteration is decided based on following two steps. In first step, computation of the minimum completion time (MCT) of each unassigned task over the processors to find the best processor, which can complete the processing of that task at earliest time. The current loads of processors (e k ) and the execution time of the task on each processor (x i,k ) are taken into considerations to take this decision. In second step, the task is selected with the minimum MCT among all unassigned tasks and assigns the task to its best processor found in the first step. Due to this task selection policy MinMin favors the assignment of tasks with lower costs in earlier iterations, and hence the assignments of tasks with higher costs are usually performed during the later iterations. These two steps can be implemented by using following algorithm. U,e,x,K

div.head: IV. PROPOSED MODIFIED HUERISTICS FOR INDEPENDENT TASK SCHEDULING
div.p: A. MinMax Algorithm MinMax, devised from MaxMin [2], [3], [9], [16], selects the task with minimum MCT and then assigns it to the processor found as per following algorithm.

div.formula: (i', k') MINMAXSELECT(U, e, x, K) A[i'] k' e k' e k' + x i',k' U U {i'} return A B. MinMax+
div.p: MinMax+ is hybrid approach resulting after combining MinMin and MinMax. MinMax+ can eliminate the drawbacks caused by MaxMin and MinMin. The MinMax+ involves a main loop that assigns a selected task to a processor in each iteration as in case of MinMin and MinMax. First it computes a task-to processor assignment according to the MinMin. The computed assignment is realized only if it does not lead to an increase in the makespan of the previous iteration. If the computed assignment increases the makespan, the task-toprocessor assignment is recomputed according to the MinMax. The MinMax+ algorithm is given below.
div.formula: U U {i'} F[i'] TRUE for k 1 to K do DELETE(Q k , i') return A
div.p: The MinMin+Init performs the necessary initializations as in MinMin+. (i', k') MINMIN+SELECT(Q, e, K)computes the task-to-processor assignment according to MinMin+. The if statement checks whether the computed assignment increases the current makespan. (i', k') MINMAXSELECT(U, e, x, K)computes the task-to-processor assignment according to MinMax. The MinMax+ differs from RASA in that the choice between MinMin and MinMax at each iteration is made in an adaptive manner, considering the current processor loads.

div.head: V. EXPERIMENTAL RESULTS AND COMPARATIVE ANALYSIS
div.p: Social-network analysis and distributed web crawling these application areas were considered from where datasets has been collected to carry out experiments. Some of the datasets can be downloaded from http://www.informatik.unitrier.de/~ley/db/, http://lemurproject.org/clueweb09/. The independent task assignment problem can occur in load balancing of parallel/distributed applications. Following table 1 shows the properties of the datasets used for experimentations.

Social network datasets are in the form of sparse graphs. Vertex in coauthorship represents an author and an edge represents the relation between two authors. Vertex in commonJob represents an employee and an edge between two vertices if the respective employees have ever worked in the same company. The coauthorship and commonJob datasets can be downloaded from DBLP http://www.informatik.unitrier.de/~ley/db/ and LinkedIn http://www.linkedin.com/. Each vertex can be considered as a task to be processed. The cost of executing cost can be taken as the degree of a vertex.

In distributed web crawling datasets, the web sites are considered as tasks, the crawlers that will download the pages in the web sites represent the processors, the number of pages in the respective web site is considered as the weight of a task. These datasets are obtained from http://lemurproject.org/clueweb09/.

The execution time obtained when the tasks are assigned to their required processor is represented by . The following table 2 shows the load imbalance values for 4-, 8-, 16-, 24-, and 32-processor assignments obtained by the existing heuristics MaxMin (MxM) and MinMin (MM) and proposed heuristics MinMax (MMx) and MinMax+ (MMx+) for different types of datasets. The bold value(s) in each row in table 2 indicate the best solution(s) in terms of load balancing performance.

div.head: VI. CONCLUSION
div.p: Performance improvements over the existing independent task assignment heuristics are analyzed and presented. The MinMax+ and MinMax are proposed, which are modified versions of MaxMin. The heuristic which the worst-case runtime complexity from O(KN 2 ) to O(KN logN) in assigning N independent tasks to K processors. The performances of algorithms are evaluated over a large number of real-life datasets. The experiments indicate that proposed heuristics runs considerably faster than existing heuristics. The use of MinMax+ for skewed datasets is recommended.
